newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition, SPD start second tax meeting.
newsitem.headline: German coalition, SPD start second tax meeting.

text.p: Negotiators from Germany's coalition government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday started a second round of cross-party talks aimed at agreeing big tax reforms to boost investment and jobs.
The two sides met at the offices of Finance Ministry Theo Waigel to try and find a compromise on government plans to slash 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes over the next two years.

Both sides found common ground on cutting corporation tax and the bottom rate of income tax at the first round of rare face-to-face talks on Monday, which were prompted by a surge in January unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933.
And they signalled ahead of the second round of talks that they were willing to compromise on Waigel's bid to cut top-rate income tax to 39 percent from 53 percent.
Heinz Schleusser, finance minister of North Rhine-Westphalia and a member of the three-strong SPD team, said a deal could be reached -- on certain conditions.
"For me the question has always been the extent to which (such a cut) would be financed through the elimination of tax breaks," Schleusser said in a radio interview.
"We have to see how far the other side is willing to go beyond that which has already been discussed, to do more."

Waigel told parliament agreement on cutting corporation tax and entry rate income tax could be a "crystallisation point" for a broad deal. But he warned that SPD reluctance to cut top income tax would not get past the constitutional court.

The meeting was delayed slightly by a parliamentary debate on a government bill which would have scrapped a capital trading tax on companies from next year. The bill passed in the Bundestag lower house, but the SPD said it would block it in the upper house.
